title: Is that right? – Putting a claim to the test
purpose: For writers with an existing nonfiction draft: define a claim that can be checked, assess sources and judge a reasoned revision in context.
notice: All dialogue and sample manuscript passages are fictional. The linked expert source was actually read for this draft. The walkthrough illustrates one possible conversation, not a completed book task or an automated fact check.

pages.label: 1 · The claim
pages.title: A sentence sounds convincing
pages.lead: A clear statement can promise more than its source supports.

blocks.text: My nonfiction draft says: “Today, early warning systems can reliably predict earthquakes.” Please check that claim. If it is inaccurate, suggest a change with sources. Do not replace anything in the manuscript yet.
I will focus first on “predict”: do you mean an announcement before an earthquake begins, or a warning once it has already started? I also need the surrounding paragraph.

The paragraph reads: “Earthquakes often catch people unprepared. Today, early warning systems can reliably predict earthquakes. This means there is enough time to reach safety before every strong earthquake.” I mean a warning before the shaking can be felt.

Then we need to check two things: what an early warning system detects, and whether there really is enough time before every strong earthquake. I will keep those questions separate so that the revision does more than swap one word.

blocks.title: The task
blocks.text: A distinction between terms and an absolute promise need checking. The full paragraph remains visible as context.

blocks.title: What this teaches
blocks.text: The follow-up changes the research task: both “predict” and “enough time before every strong earthquake” need checking.

pages.label: 2 · The source
pages.title: What does the source support?
pages.lead: A suitable source must address the particular claim made in the text.

blocks.text: The Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich distinguishes earthquake prediction from early warning in its FAQ. It explains that early warning processes measurements of an earthquake that has already started. A warning can reach more distant areas before the shaking arrives there. [Q1]
Is that a research study? And does it let me keep the word “reliably”?

It is an expert overview from the seismological service, not an individual original research study. It suits the basic distinction. However, it does not establish an overall reliability rate or a promise for every location. For that, we would need to examine a particular system and its performance data.

blocks.title: Source and scope
rows: Q1 · Publisher
Swiss Seismological Service (SED) at ETH Zurich; institutional expert information.
Location
FAQ “Can earthquakes be predicted?”, introduction and the “Earthquake early warning” section.
Currency
Accessed on 10 November 2026. The page consulted does not display a publication or revision date. The access date is not a publication date.
Scope
Basic principles and limits of early warning; not an exhaustive review of systems or recent research.

blocks.title: Actually consulted
blocks.text: The expert information is real and linked below. The conversation is simulated. No second confirming source or complete literature review is claimed.

pages.label: 3 · Finding and proposal
pages.title: Make the claim more precise
pages.lead: A useful revision explains which overstatement it removes.

blocks.text: The sentence conflates prediction and early warning. The conclusion about “every” earthquake also goes beyond the source. I suggest: “Earthquake early warning systems detect an earthquake that has already started. Under suitable conditions, they can issue a warning before stronger shaking reaches a more distant location.” [Q1]
That is more precise. But I do not want readers to assume they can always react in time, wherever they are.

Then let us add an explicit limit: “This does not guarantee a timely warning at every location.” We would remove the original final sentence. The source describes a limit related to distance; I will not add a specific number of seconds without reference to a particular system.

blocks.title: From finding to revision
rows: “reliably predict”
Replace with detection of an earthquake that has already started.
“enough time before every…”
Remove; a warning at every location is not guaranteed.
New figures or success rates
Do not add: this task has not established sufficient evidence for them.

blocks.title: Proposed change, not yet applied
blocks.text: The source supports a more precise explanation. It does not become evidence for another blanket assurance of safety.

pages.label: 4 · In context
pages.title: The author decides on the paragraph
pages.lead: Once the facts have been checked, the whole paragraph needs to work again.

blocks.text: Include that limit. Keep the opening. Show me the full paragraph with a source reference at the relevant sentence ending.

A revised sample paragraph: “Earthquakes often catch people unprepared. Early warning systems detect an earthquake that has already started and, under suitable conditions, can issue a warning before stronger shaking reaches more distant locations. This does not guarantee a timely warning at every location. [Q1]”
That is the passage I want to use. I would also like a brief explanation of prediction alongside it, but not squeezed into this paragraph.
The desired version of the paragraph has now been selected within this dialogue. The additional explanation remains a separate task. I have not changed a book file or formally approved a section.

blocks.title: Editorial review
blocks.text: The full paragraph has been reread for terminology, reasoning and readability. The absolute promise is removed; the limitation appears alongside the explanation of the method.

blocks.title: Sample manuscript text
blocks.text: The sample is fictional. [Q1] is an unambiguous working reference here, not an established citation style for the book.

pages.label: 5 · Result and limits
pages.title: What was checked — and what remains open?
pages.lead: A review note makes the scope of the work clear.

blocks.title: Review note for the simulated passage
rows: Text reviewed
The full three-sentence original paragraph from stage 1 and the revised version from stage 4.
Finding
Prediction and early warning were conflated; the conclusion promised warning time for every strong earthquake.
Revision
Clarified the terms, removed the blanket promise, added a limit and a working reference.
Evidence
One institutional expert source actually consulted; accessed on 10 November 2026. No systematic literature review.
Open items
The separate explanation of prediction; a consistent citation style; current technical evidence if specific systems are discussed.
Result
Editorial review passed with notes for this sample passage. No judgement about the entire book, no saving and no formal approval.

blocks.title: Apply this to your own text
blocks.text: Define the claim, read a suitable source, separate findings from proposals, review the whole paragraph and record the author’s decision.
